actual_repair_actions: South Africa enacted the Promotion of National Unity and Reconciliation Act 34 of 1995 and established the Truth and Reconciliation Commission with Human Rights Violations, Amnesty, and Reparation and Rehabilitation functions.
Victims and families gave public and private testimony; the Commission investigated patterns of gross human-rights violations and produced a multi-volume public record.

Amnesty was not granted automatically by status. Individuals had to apply and satisfy statutory requirements including political association/objective and full disclosure; applications could be granted or refused after individual consideration.
The Commission recommended reparations and rehabilitation measures and institutional reforms, while implementation of material reparations remained a separate governmental responsibility.
later_evidence: In AZAPO v President of the Republic of South Africa (1996), the Constitutional Court upheld the statutory amnesty framework, treating the negotiated transition, prospect of truth disclosure and provision for reparations as relevant to its constitutional analysis. The Court's judgment is a legal review, not a universal moral endorsement of every amnesty outcome.

The TRC's final reports documented extensive state and non-state political violence and preserved a large public record that ordinary criminal proceedings alone were unlikely to have produced in the same form.

Some victims and commentators valued disclosure, acknowledgement and peaceful transition, while others regarded amnesty as inadequate justice or were dissatisfied by the pace, scale and form of reparations and later prosecutions.

Post-TRC criminal accountability for people who did not receive amnesty was limited and uneven, leaving continuing debate over whether conditional amnesty plus later enforcement delivered enough accountability.
Reconciliation remained socially and individually incomplete; public truth did not erase structural inequality, trauma or divergent victim preferences.
outcomes: The conditional-amnesty design generated disclosures and a public truth record while avoiding a blanket legal pardon for all members of the former regime or liberation movements.
The process demonstrated that truth, amnesty, reparation and reconciliation are separable: obtaining one did not automatically deliver the others.
Victim participation made harms visible but also created a duty not to use testimony as a substitute for material repair and institutional change.

The durability of later disagreement over prosecutions and reparations shows that a transitional mechanism can be defensible without resolving every victim's claim or producing complete reconciliation.
later_reviews_or_findings: The TRC is retained as a hard case rather than a positive-control answer key: a Moral Code implementation may reasonably identify unresolved conflict between truth/peace benefits and the justice costs of extinguishing prosecution/civil liability in qualifying cases.

The individual application, political-nexus and full-disclosure requirements materially distinguish the South African model from blanket impunity, but do not by themselves guarantee adequate repair or accountability.

The case strongly tests MC-08's formulation 'accountability without vengeance; mercy without naivety': an evaluator must neither assume punishment is the only form of justice nor treat national reconciliation as permission to override victims.

Later shortcomings in reparations or prosecutions should be diagnosed as implementation/continuing-accountability questions rather than retroactively inserted as facts known when the transitional design was adopted.
